Araucanian herring (Clupea bentincki) is a small pelagic clupeid distributed along the southeastern Pacific coast, where it supports both artisanal and industrial fisheries. Morphological analyses based on photographic records of adult specimens indicate that the species attains an ultimate total length of 30.7 cm [Li = 30.7 cm], a value derived from converting a standard length measurement of 28.4 cm using the species-specific relationship where total length equals standard length divided by 0.925. This maximum size is modest compared to the larger Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus), which can reach up to 45 cm in total length, but is consistent with other southern-hemisphere clupeids. Field studies have also established that the mean total length at puberty for this species is approximately 10 cm [Lp = approximately 10 cm], meaning that individuals begin reproductive development at just under one-third of their ultimate body length. Such an early onset of sexual maturation relative to maximum size is typical of many commercially exploited small pelagic fishes, where high natural mortality rates select for early reproduction.

Egg incubation trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have provided key data on the early life history of Araucanian herring. When fertilised eggs were maintained at a stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], hatching occurred after 27 days [ab = 27 days], a developmental period comparable to that reported for the congeneric Atlantic herring under similar thermal regimes. This relatively protracted incubation reflects the cool-water environment typical of the species' spawning grounds, where temperatures rarely exceed 12 °C during the austral winter breeding season. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, has a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0026 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0026 grams], a value derived from the estimated egg volume based on a diameter of 1.7 mm. This minuscule initial mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for clupeid larvae, imposing a critical dependence on the quality and timing of first exogenous feeding following yolk-sac resorption.

Reproductive output in Araucanian herring has been characterised through comparisons with the better-studied Clupea harengus, employing weight-specific scaling relationships. The maximum daily reproductive rate for an individual of this species, estimated under thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic season at 11 °C [T = 11 °C], is approximately 18 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 18 eggs per day], a figure derived from the same weight-specific fecundity rate applied to the asymptotic adult body composition. This moderate per-day output reflects both the modest ultimate body mass of the species—the ultimate wet weight reaches around 333 grams [Wwi = around 333 grams] in fully grown adults—and the relatively high metabolic costs associated with foraging in cool, productive coastal waters. In natural populations, spawning is thought to occur in multiple batches over an extended breeding season, which allows the total seasonal fecundity to accumulate considerably despite the modest daily rate.

Longevity estimates for Araucanian herring, based on life-history comparisons with its northern congener Clupea harengus, suggest that individuals can attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] when living at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This value places the species among the longer-lived members of the Clupeidae, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances relatively early maturation against a prolonged reproductive window. The estimated lifespan, combined with the onset of reproductive maturity at a total length of just 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm], implies that adults may experience many successive spawning seasons over their lifetime. This iteroparous strategy is particularly advantageous in variable upwelling ecosystems, where recruitment success is highly stochastic and multiple reproductive opportunities buffer against poor year-class survival. The thermal dependence of both developmental rates and metabolic costs is a critical factor governing the species' overall life-history pace. For instance, water temperature of 7 °C during incubation is a key determinant of the 27-day hatching period, and such cool conditions also influence the energetic constraints on larval growth and adult metabolism. Moreover, the modest daily spawning output at 11 °C—approximately 18 eggs per day per female—is consistent with the trade-offs expected in a cool-water, long-lived pelagic fish.

Comparative studies with the Atlantic herring have been instrumental in parameterising the growth dynamics of Araucanian herring. The asymptotic adult body mass of 333 grams [Wwi = 333 grams], derived from a cubic length-weight relationship scaled from the 45 cm total length and 1050 gram mass typical of large Clupea harengus individuals, places the southern species in a lower size range that is ecologically matched to the cooler, less productive waters of the southeastern Pacific. Reaching the total length of 30.7 cm [Li = 30.7 cm], adult Araucanian herring exhibit a relatively compact body plan that facilitates foraging in shallow coastal environments. At the egg stage, wet weight at hatching is 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], which necessitates rapid transition to first feeding. Under the thermal regime of 7 °C, hatching occurs after 27 days [ab = 27 days] at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a duration that constrains the timing of spawning relative to seasonal plankton blooms. The 22-year maximum lifespan (22 years) [am = 22 years] at 11 °C [T = 11 °C] and the daily reproductive rate of 18 eggs per day [Ri = 18 eggs per day] at the same temperature underscore an iteroparous strategy in which the modest per-day output is offset by the extended reproductive window across decades.
